title: 'Rubik's Cube molecule' puts the stretch in next-gen semiconductors
excerpt: Plastics that are both good at conducting electricity and flexible enough to stretch and bend are already being used in cell phones with folding screens. But because the rigid crystals they contain—which help with conductivity—aren't naturally flexible, they still often crack. Now, researchers from the University of Toronto have found a way to increase the stretchiness of these materials while maintaining their ability to conduct electricity, potentially opening new uses in medicine and biology.
content_html:
Plastics that are both good at conducting electricity and flexible enough to stretch and bend are already being used in cell phones with folding screens. But because the rigid crystals they contain—which help with conductivity—aren't naturally flexible, they still often crack. Now, researchers from the University of Toronto have found a way to increase the stretchiness of these materials while maintaining their ability to conduct electricity, potentially opening new uses in medicine and biology.

"Most semiconductors in the electronics you might have in your computer or cell phone are made of silicon, which is a hard, rigid and brittle metalloid," says Shine Huang, a Ph.D. student doing research on conductive plastics at the University of Toronto under professor Helen Tran. "But if we want to create electronics we can put inside the human body—for things like pacemakers or prosthetics—we need materials that are softer and stretchable and can conform to biological tissue."

The research is published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition.

A shape-shifting molecule adds flexibility

Huang experimented with an organic molecule called bullvalene, which he likens to a Rubik's Cube because it's constantly shifting and transforming. He found that, by adding bullvalene to a plastic semiconductor, the resulting material became much more flexible. In its initial form, the plastic acts like a bundle of straight wires, he says; adding bullvalene broke up the plastic's crystal structure and transformed it into a loose bundle of wires.

Huang found the plastic now had much greater flexibility; it could stretch more than twice as far without cracking—yet still conducted electricity nearly as well as before.

"I was expecting it (bullvalene) to tremendously worsen its potential as a semiconductor, because they generally have to be quite crystalline and packed together nicely so that electrical current can pass through it well," he says. "But even though there was a lot of chaos introduced, it still had good electrical properties."

Smaller crystals preserve conductivity

Huang brought his sample material to the Canadian Light Source (CLS) at the University of Saskatchewan to figure out why bullvalene was able to increase his material's flexibility without losing conductivity. "The CLS let me really examine the 'why,'" he says. "It let me determine the crystal properties of this plastic."

The ultrabright synchrotron light revealed that crystals are still present in the flexible conductive plastic but are a lot smaller than in typical plastic semiconductors, allowing it to stretch while still conducting electricity.

Huang is continuing to explore how bullvalene could be used in other plastics, not just conductive ones. "I think there is a lot of exploration still to be done with this specific molecule as the chaotic nature of its constant rearrangement could drastically change other material properties," he says.

Publication details

Shine H. Huang et al., Fluxional Monomers Remodel Crystallinity at Low Loadings in Diketopyrrolopyrrole Co‐Thienothiophene Conjugated Polymers, Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2026). DOI: 10.1002/anie.3478969
